headline: Intel & AMD sign server CPU deals with China amid 40%+ price hikes
summary: Intel and AMD are reportedly entering longer-term purchase commitments with Chinese customers for server processors, as prices for some chips have already surged over 40% this year.
details: Intel and AMD are reportedly signing extended purchase agreements with Chinese server customers for data center processors, according to Reuters. Prices for some server CPUs in China have already increased by more than 40% since the beginning of the year, with further monthly increases of over 10% being reported.

These agreements primarily guarantee purchase volumes for approximately one year without fixing prices. This structure leaves Chinese cloud providers and internet companies fully exposed to market fluctuations, which have already driven up the cost of some CPUs significantly.

Some customers have explored commitments extending to two years or longer, with deals covering only unit volumes. This means buyers are not guaranteed price protection and may face extended delivery times, but they secure a place in the supply queue.

Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger mentioned in March that the company was pursuing long-term agreements due to spiking server CPU demand, noting that demand "continues to run ahead of supply." This strategy now spans U.S. hyperscalers and Chinese buyers alike.

Lead times for server CPUs have dramatically increased, with reports from March indicating average lead times stretching from one to two weeks to eight to 12 weeks or longer. Intel's CFO previously stated that unmet Xeon demand "starts with a B."

The surge in demand is largely driven by agentic AI workloads, where inference and orchestration tasks are increasing the need for server CPUs. AMD has raised its server CPU market forecast to over $120 billion by 2030 based on this trend.

While Chinese buyers are restricted from acquiring the most advanced AI accelerators due to U.S. export controls, Intel's Xeon and AMD's EPYC server CPUs are not subject to these restrictions, making them crucial components of China's AI infrastructure that can still be purchased.
